A sign for the front fence.

Start here

Simplest

Both reference signs do the same thing, and it is subtraction rather than a style. One type block at the top, one at the bottom, and a void doing the rest. The Georgie Shepherd panel goes furthest: the name, the words INTERIOR STUDIO, and nothing else at all. No phone, no address, no code. The Laura Abrams A-frame keeps a hairline row of services and a small code, but still gives most of the panel to empty white.

So these give up the headline and the services line, and keep one or two contact routes and nothing more. Square corners, since both references are square and both hang rather than sit.

Each layout comes in two: without a code, which is the truer reading of the references, and with one. The code is 60 mm on every version, the same size as the rest of the set, so nothing is given up on scanning to keep the panel quiet.

What that costs, plainly: a panel with one contact route and no code is a brand statement rather than a lead generator. It is a completely legitimate choice, and the Georgie Shepherd sign is proof, but it is a different job from the one the earlier rounds were doing. The versions with a code are the compromise, and they cost the composition very little.

The round before

Boutique, four ways

Less corporate, more boutique. What reads corporate in the earlier panels is specific and removable: everything stacked on a dead-centre axis and evenly weighted, a services list separated by middle dots, an ENQUIRIES label sitting over a bold sans number, colour fields running edge to edge, and five or six pieces of information competing for the same space.

So these four drop the services list, set the number in Cormorant Garamond rather than bold Inter, use asymmetry or a contained panel instead of full-width bands, and simply carry less. The headline moves to italic lower case, which is the boutique voice and also keeps the no-sentence-case rule. No new colours: same champagne, cream, warm charcoal and gold. The boutique quality comes from space, asymmetry and type rather than from anything added.

Spine comes in four: light or warm dark ground, headline in italic lower case or in roman capitals. The services list moved onto the spine rather than being dropped, so the information is still there for anyone standing at the fence, without a middle-dot row running across the composition.

Two things to weigh. The serif number reads at roughly 2.4 to 2.7 m against 3.3 m for the softened set, so these are gate-and-doorstep signs rather than across-the-street ones. And Cormorant sets numerals as old-style figures, where the 4 and the 7 drop below the line, which is a large part of why the number looks elegant here and also makes it fractionally slower to read at a glance.

Latest round of changes, applied across the whole set: the QR is up from 46 to 60 mm, the website, handle and licence number are up roughly a sixth, and the spine has gone from 9 to 11 point.

The spine question

No, the spine will not be read from a car

Worth being straight about it. At 11 point the spine has a 6.9 mm cap height, which is comfortable at about 0.8 m. It is a detail for someone standing at the fence, and rotated type costs a head tilt on top of that.

But the honest version of the answer is bigger than the spine. Nothing on a 400 mm wide panel carries a services list to a passing car. A 10 m read needs about 85 mm of cap height, and INTERIOR DESIGN alone at that size runs well over a metre wide. Set horizontally in the middle of the panel it would be no more readable from a car than it is on the spine, only less elegant. A driver at 40 km/h has one or two seconds of usable glance and takes in a single element in that time.

On these panels that element is the mark, at 86 mm cap, readable at around 10 m. That is the thing doing the work from the road, and it is doing it well. The spine, the number and the QR are all for people who have already slowed down or stopped. If services genuinely need to reach traffic, that is a second and much larger panel, not a change to this one.

The round before

Softer, four ways, all in capitals

Monolith was the right direction but read as too structured. The structure in it comes from four things: a rectangular keyline, a flat near-black ground, sans-serif capitals tracked wide across every line, and lines stacked at even intervals. All four are dialled back here. The frame is gone. The ground is a warm charcoal that reads brown-black in daylight instead of switched-off-screen black. Rules are shorter, lighter and round-capped, the number drops from SemiBold to Medium, and the spacing between groups is now larger than the spacing within them. The corners are cut at a 20 mm radius, which is a router setting rather than artwork, and does more for softness than anything on the panel.

Capitals return in the headline, but as Cormorant Garamond at display size rather than tracked sans, which is a different animal: the serif does the work and the tracking only opens it up. The rule is applied down the whole panel: the services line and the enquiries label follow the same rule. Capitals need letter-spacing to breathe and run wide, so the headline breaks over two lines at 40 point, which lands on a 25 mm cap height. The web address, the licence number and the Instagram handle stay as they are, being literal strings rather than styled copy.

The one cost of the softening: the lighter number weight gives up roughly 0.3 m of read distance. That is what softer buys.

Dark or light

I would go light, and keep dark for the door

Dark is the more premium read on screen, which is why it is where these started. Outdoors on a residential street, light wins on four practical counts. It holds contrast in direct sun, where a dark panel flares and goes flat. It hides the dust and pollen that settle on a site sign within a week, which a dark panel shows as a grey film. It stays cooler, so the panel is less prone to bowing on a north-facing fence. And it separates from the fence itself, since most Adelaide frontages are dark colourbond, hedging or brick, and a near-black panel disappears into all three.

Champagne also happens to be the softer of the two, which is the thing being asked for. Softened Light is my recommendation. Keep Softened Dark for a smaller plaque by the door and for portfolio photography, where it is unbeatable.

Second pass

Four more, against the style guide and the signage rules

These add what the first pass missed. The style guide names Cormorant Garamond as the display face and the first five used Inter throughout, so the serif appears here, along with the full six-colour palette and the clear-space rule of one monogram height around the mark. The signage research contributed the rest: one dominant message per panel, roughly 25 mm of cap height per 3 m of viewing distance, light-on-dark or dark-on-light only, and enough empty field that the mark lands before the detail does.

QR codes

Two sets of artwork, one per destination

Every layout is generated twice. The website address is already set in type on all twenty-eight panels, so the Instagram code is arguably the more useful scan: it takes a passer-by straight to photographs of the work. Every panel above shows the Instagram set.

Instagram

instagram.com/lkdesignandbuild, with the camera mark knocked out of the centre. Error correction steps up to H, which recovers 30% of the code, so the mark costs it nothing. Caption on the panel reads @lkdesignandbuild. Now 60 mm, which puts a module at 1.33 mm and takes the comfortable scan distance to around 600 mm.

Website

lkdesignandbuild.com.au, plain, error correction Q. Files are the -web set. Use these if the sign should send people to the portfolio pages rather than the feed.

All fifty-six codes were decoded from the finished 300 dpi artwork to confirm they scan. A useful check on the enlargement: at 46 mm a reader could only find the code once the crop was narrowed to the code itself, and at 60 mm every one is found in the full panel image. Dropping https:// from the encoded address would buy another 10% in module size, but some scanners then treat it as plain text rather than a link, so the scheme stays. Both are drawn as vector modules and stay sharp at any size.

Recommendation

Where I'd land

Kerbside is the one I'd print. It gives the number the largest cap height a 400 mm panel can physically carry, keeps the mark and the serif line above it, and holds the highest contrast of the nine. It does the job a site sign is for without the sign looking like it is shouting.

Nightfall if the brief is really about presence rather than enquiries. It is the most restrained and the best to photograph for the portfolio. Editorial is the distinctive one, and the closest to how the brand actually speaks; it trades about 1.5 m of number legibility for that.

They are not exclusive. The same artwork scales cleanly to a larger panel, so a common pattern is Kerbside on the street frontage and Nightfall by the door.

Legibility

What a 400 mm panel can and cannot do

Sign trade rule of thumb: about 25 mm of cap height per 3 m of comfortable reading distance.

ElementCap heightComfortable read
LK mark, largest layouts85–94 mm10–11 m
LK mark, Kerbside57 mm7 m
Phone, Kerbside36 mm4.4 m
Phone, typical24–33 mm3–4 m
Serif headline22–33 mm2.7–4 m

At 400 mm wide the number cannot be made to read from a passing car. A 10 m read needs about 85 mm of cap height, which would set 0401 061 246 around 770 mm wide. This is a footpath and driveway sign: the mark reads from across the street, the number reads from the fence. A second, larger panel is the answer if car traffic matters.

Production

Files and fixing

print-pdf/Send this to the printer. 406 × 606 mm, vector, type outlined.
print-svg/Same artwork, editable.
print-png/300 dpi fallback, 4795 × 7157 px.
preview/Trim-only SVG and 900 px PNG for review and email.
guides/Trim, safe area and hole positions. Reference only, never send to print.
PRODUCTION-SPEC.mdFull spec: colour build, print method, fixing, pre-press checklist.

Each option appears twice in every folder, as -insta and -web. Fifty-six files per format.

Fixing: four Ø6 mm holes, centres 30 mm in from each corner, plus two optional at mid-height for a temporary mesh fence. Those positions were checked against all twenty-eight layouts: they land in flat colour and clear every piece of type. On the softened set the corners are routed at a 20 mm radius, which only cuts the corner squares, so the 30 mm hole centres stay well clear of the curve. Black nylon cable ties or stainless with black cup washers. 3 mm ACM at this size needs no frame.

Ask for a matt or satin anti-glare finish and a rich black build on the dark grounds. The gold is a warm tan, not a metallic. Closest reference is Pantone 465 C, and it is worth a proof strip.
